title: Thunderstruck
author: Erik Larson
target_audience: Readers interested in historical nonfiction and true crime
Fans of narrative history blending multiple storylines
Individuals curious about the development of technology
Those who enjoy dramatic real-life mysteries
core_themes: The impact and promise of technological innovation
Pursuit of scientific discovery and the human cost
Connections between seemingly unrelated historical events
Persistence and obsession in both crime and science
primary_purpose: To intertwine the dramatic history of Marconi's invention of wireless telegraphy with the notorious Crippen murder case, illustrating how technological innovation can intersect with human stories and reshape the world.

structure_format.organization: Alternating, parallel narratives that eventually converge—one following Guglielmo Marconi's quest to develop wireless communication, the other the infamous crime and investigation involving Dr. Hawley Crippen
features: Interweaving timelines and converging story arcs

key_concepts_lessons: Scientific advancements can have unforeseen societal implications.
Communication technology shrinks the world and transforms how news—and justice—move.
Obsession, whether with invention or relationships, can yield both brilliance and tragedy.
Historical events are often interconnected in ways not immediately apparent.
Media coverage and rapid communication play pivotal roles in public perception of crime and innovation.
notable_features: Vivid evocation of Edwardian era settings
Seamless blend of scientific history and crime narrative
Humanizes key figures while illuminating technological shifts
cultural_historical_context: Set in late Victorian and Edwardian England, the book captures a world on the cusp of modern communication, when the invention of wireless telegraphy synchronized with a sensational murder case, illuminating an age of media frenzy and technological optimism.
reception_impact: Critical and commercial success, acclaimed for storytelling prowess
Praised for its research depth and engaging narrative
Frequently used as an example of successful popular history writing
Sparked renewed interest in both Marconi and the Crippen case
comparable_titles: The Devil in the White City by Erik Larson
The Poisoner's Handbook by Deborah Blum
Destiny of the Republic by Candice Millard
The Ghost Map by Steven Johnson
